item.title: Big Harry's Automotive
item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
If you have car trouble in the town of Clearview, you go to Big Harry’s Automotive. Besides Big Harry’s being the only repair shop in town, Big Harry himself could fix anything. In fact, I’d never heard of someone bringing their car in for repairs and leaving without the problem resolved.

Despite his immense skill, Big Harry had some unusual policies.

For one thing, he never answered the phone. Nor did he consult with customers before servicing their vehicles. In fact, I’m not sure anyone had ever actually seen him leave the garage.

But everyone in Clearview knew the process.

You’d drop your car off. Then you’d leave.

Eventually, your phone would ring.

“Car’s done. Two hundred dollars.”

Click.

That was it. Every time.

And it was always two hundred dollars, no matter the job. A transmission replacement? Two hundred. An oil change? Two hundred. Replacing a missing lug nut? Two hundred.

Some people thought the arrangement sounded unfair as they slipped their checks through the little slot in the garage door.

But the other strange thing about Big Harry was that he never cashed any of them.

If you pressed your eye to the slot and looked inside, you could see the checks piled nearly three feet high on the dirty tile floor.

You might read this and think: What a lucky town. A mechanic who works for free.

But there’s always a price.

And I had to pay it the day I walked into Big Harry’s garage.

Back then I drove a blue Ford Taurus that was always breaking down. Unfortunately, this particular breakdown happened at the worst possible time. It was Friday morning, and the next day I had to drive a couple of hours away for a wedding I was in.

I considered gambling on the car and making the trip anyway, but the noise coming from under the hood sounded like the kind of problem you can’t responsibly ignore.

So around mid-morning, I parked the Taurus in Big Harry’s lot and hoped he’d get to it before the end of the day.

Luckily, my workplace was within walking distance.

I never got the call during my shift, but around six o’clock I headed back over to the garage. There wasn’t much else I could do.

When I arrived, I was relieved to see my car no longer sitting in the parking lot. Maybe he was working on it now. But for all I knew, he could’ve decided to leave it half-finished until morning.

Either way, I was stuck. Home was too far to walk, and I desperately needed him to understand how urgent this was.

Eventually, my determination outweighed my hesitation.

I decided I was going to walk inside and speak to Big Harry myself.

I pulled open the glass door and stepped inside. The waiting area was dim; a thick layer of dust matted every surface. An open door led to the back, where I could hear the sound of ratchets and the song “Plush” by Stone Temple Pilots.

“Excuse me…” I shouted hesitantly into the garage.

No answer.

Slowly, I crept closer, peeking my head through the doorway.

It looked like you’d expect an automotive repair shop to look. In fact, it looked far cleaner and more organized than the lobby. It almost put me at ease… until I saw Big Harry.

“Big” was not in any way an accurate description.

Big Harry was larger than I previously believed any human could be.

He sat next to my blue Ford Taurus, and beyond being just as large as the car itself, parts of him billowed over the hood, parts that human beings just don’t have. I stood frozen in the doorway.

Just as my mind was recovering, Big Harry looked up. His eyes, dead and emotionless, fixed on me.

He stared for a moment. Then, in that voice I’d only ever heard say, “Car’s done. Two hundred dollars,” I heard something different.

“Half inch. Deep socket.”

The words registered in my mind, but I found myself dissociated from their meaning and context. There were no real thoughts, no deliberation, but my body responded.

I walked into the garage, past Big Harry, and over to the large red toolbox along the far wall.

As if I had done it a million times, my hand moved across the massive array of sockets, picked one up, and returned to Big Harry.

He didn’t take the socket.

He took my entire arm.

As I looked on in shock, I saw I was no longer holding the socket.

My hand was the socket.

He gripped my forearm, yanked me toward the wheel well, and connected the socket to a bolt. Somehow, I felt the coldness of the bolt as I made contact. Even so, the strongest sensation was the smell: grease and pungent body odor.

As Big Harry cranked on my arm, a ratcheting sound emanated from where my wrist would be.

It’s hard to explain exactly how I felt. It was as if there were two of me. One part was stoic, automatic, as if this were the most normal thing in the world. The other, however…the one that couldn’t seem to find its voice, was terrified. Terrified not only to be so close to such an unnatural creature, but to understand firsthand what sort of power he had over me.

When he was finished, he let go of my arm, and I stood there, unable to move. I could feel my body trembling, my breath halting, but no matter what I told myself to do, it just wasn’t happening.

Until I heard him speak again.

“Twenty millimeter.”

That’s when my body moved again, back toward the toolbox.

I looked down at my one hand, which had become something like a wrench with a half inch socket attached, and watched as my other, still-normal hand reached for the twenty-millimeter socket.

I finally found my voice.

“No… don’t,” I whispered.

But it didn’t matter. My hand grasped the socket.

And right before my eyes, my hand was no more.

My legs carried me back to Big Harry. He repeated the same process, grabbing my forearm and extracting a bolt from beneath my car with it.

I managed to ask, “Why are you doing this?”

I can’t be sure he replied, but if he did, it was nothing more than a grunt and a shrug.

Then he spoke again.

“One and three-quarters deep well. Impact.”

I watched him move toward a different part of the toolbox.

And despite my fear, I wondered what would happen next, now that both my hands were no longer available.

The realization sent me into a full panic as I felt my mouth opening and my head slowly turning toward the row of black sockets.

I struggled with all my might to keep my body from obeying Big Harry’s commands.

There was nothing I could do.

I let out a garbled scream as the socket entered my mouth.

I was sure my head had transformed into something unnatural, but I could still see.

I walked back to Big Harry, who took hold of the back of my head and forced my mouth onto a large bolt. I felt him press something against the back of my head, followed by a loud clinking noise, and then we both began to turn.

He pulled my head away.

The bolt was still in my mouth.

I found myself placing a new part somewhere in the wheel well.

Then he used the same sockets in reverse order, putting the big one back on and then the two smaller ones.

Finally, the wheel returned to its place, and he pressed a button hanging from a nearby cable. The car lowered a few inches.

I’m not sure exactly how, but Big Harry moved away from the car, backing up a few feet and looking it over with another grunting noise.

Slowly, he turned his head toward me, his eyes still lacking any semblance of humanity, and grunted:

“Car’s done. Thanks for the help.”

Suddenly, I had control of my body again.

I looked in my rearview mirror and found my face was exactly as it had been before.

But ever since that night, whenever I grip anything too tightly, I swear I can feel something inside my wrist clicking.

item.title: My New Sister. Pt.2
item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
I stared at Rachel for a moment, searching for the right words, but she yawned and stretched dramatically.

“Well, Elliot,” she said, “I’m sure you’ll remember me before too long.”

She pulled back the covers of my bed, rested her head on the pillow, and closed her eyes.

“Do you mind getting the light, little bro?” she asked after another exaggerated yawn.

What could I do?

I gathered my things from the floor, turned out the lights, and lay down. Rachel was snoring within minutes, and I just lay there, trying to make sense of the entire strange situation. I stared into the darkness, wide-eyed, half-wondering if she might get up and attack me in her sleep—not that that would make any sense either.

Then I noticed it: a faint, very faint reddish glow leaking through a crack between two boxes under my bed.

What could it be?

I racked my brain for anything I owned that might emit a light like that.

And then I remembered the box—the one I’d received from the Christmas carolers a few years back. I’d never been able to open it, so it had just sat under my bed, forgotten.

Though I couldn’t see it directly, I grew certain it was the source of the glow.

Part of me wanted to crawl over and find it right then, but there was too much junk in the way. I had no hope of locating it quietly in the dark.

So I decided to wait.

Now there was one more thing on my mind, keeping me from sleep. The last time I checked the tiny digital clock on my bedside table, it was past 1 a.m. Eventually, though, I must have drifted off.

When my alarm woke me the next morning, I was groggy. But as soon as I took in my surroundings, my heart leapt.

Rachel!

I’d forgotten she was home.

She was still stirring from the alarm. I leaned over the side of the bed and gave her a quick hug.

Her eyes stayed closed.

“So you remember me now?” she mumbled.

“How could I forget?” I said.

There wasn’t much time to catch up. I got out of bed, made it—easier than usual, since the mattress was on the floor—ate breakfast, got dressed, and headed out the door with a promise that we’d talk after school.

And just like that, I was in my car, on my way.

It was a perfectly normal day until fifth period.

Beth and I met in the outdoor courtyard for lunch. The first thing I told her, once we sat down, was that my sister, Rachel was back from Botswana.

The confusion on her face was immediate.

“You have a sister?” she asked.

The words ‘of course I do’ were already halfway out of my mouth when my mind snapped back into place. That small resistance to the illusion was enough. I remembered everything.

Including the box under my bed—the one I’d meant to grab first thing that morning. The one I hoped Rachel hadn’t found.

“Oh. No,” I moaned.

I packed up my lunch in a rush, muttered something about needing to go home, and stood to leave.

Beth grabbed my arm. “Let me come with you,” she said—clearly having no idea what was going on, but just as clearly not wanting to miss it.

I shrugged, and we hurried out to my car.

I did my best to explain what was going on to Beth on the car ride over, but none of it made sense to me; how could it make sense to someone else?

We rushed through the door, past Rachel and my parents sitting down in the living room and into my room. I knelt beside my bed and tossed the piles of junk out of the way. Soon the entire space under my bed was empty. And the box was nowhere to be found.

item.title: A tumor is trying to kill me. But it isn't mine.
item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
Scroll to the bottom for some freebies.

A few weeks ago, a patient came into my practice exhibiting strange behavior, even for someone with a brain tumor.

He was a young man, and according to his parents, completely normal before the onset of symptoms. Over the course of a month or two, however, they said he had undergone drastic personality changes. His food preferences shifted, the way he spoke changed, and even the way he dressed became unfamiliar.

It was difficult for me to measure the extent of these changes. I hadn’t known him before all this, and while he was clearly different, at least by his parents’ account, he seemed composed and in his right mind. Still, they described episodes of extreme anger that I was fortunate not to witness in those early visits.

I ordered a series of scans and, unsurprisingly, discovered a meningioma. It appeared to be pressing against the frontal lobe. Personality shifts are not unusual with this type of tumor, but I had never seen anything so comprehensive. Typically, the changes are limited to irritability or depressive symptoms.

Even so, I was confident that removing the tumor would resolve the issue.

At first, the young man was friendly during our appointments. But once the tumor was identified and we began planning its removal, his attitude toward me soured.

“You’re making a big mistake,” he said one day during a pre-op consultation. “You’d better leave me alone.”

I knew he wasn’t fully himself, but I tried to reason with him.

“If I leave you alone,” I said, “this tumor will continue to grow and eventually take over your body.”

“That’s what I want,” he shouted.

He gripped the arms of his chair, his face reddening with anger. But he never stood, never made any move toward violence. Soon enough, the consultation ended.

His instability worsened on the day of the procedure. He fought the staff to the point that we were forced to sedate him before administering general anesthesia.

The procedure itself was routine, at least at first.

It wasn’t until I reached the tumor that something felt off.

As I began excising it, I had the distinct sensation that something was pressing back against my instruments. From my angle, I couldn’t see the area directly, but through the imaging feed, it almost looked as though the mass was moving.

I noticed it once or twice. Not enough to cause real alarm.

Otherwise, the surgery was unremarkable.

I spoke with my OR team, mentioned I’d be going to a baseball game later that night. That kind of small talk is normal during procedures. I know it unsettles people to imagine surgeons chatting while someone’s skull is open, but that’s how it is.

Once the tumor was removed, we closed him up and moved him to recovery.

I was particularly interested in how the procedure would affect him, so as soon as I heard he was conscious, I went to see him.

He was still groggy from the anesthesia, but it was immediately clear I was speaking to a different person. His voice had changed. His mannerisms were different. Most notably, he was no longer threatening me.

I considered it a success.

I sent the tumor for biopsy, finished my shift, and went to the baseball game.

The next day, the threats began.

When I arrived at work, I found the words you’re dead scratched into my office door.

I contacted hospital administration, who in turn contacted the police. My entire morning was consumed with questions and paperwork. I tried to remain calm, but the truth is, I was shaken. I couldn’t understand why anyone would want to harm me.

At first, I convinced myself it was a prank.

That lasted until I checked my email.

There was a message from an unknown sender. The body contained the same words that had been carved into my door, repeated hundreds of times.

you’re dead

More calls followed. More reports. And with them, the creeping realization that someone, somewhere, truly wanted me dead.

I thought about leaving work then and there, but concluded that I was in just as much danger no matter where I went. At least at work there were security guards—and half the hospital knew about what was going on.

The only distraction came after lunch, when Hannah, our resident pathologist knocked on my door with information from the tumor from the day before. I had always liked Hannah, and while her coming up for a face-to-face chat was abnormal. I read it as indication that the tumor contained something interesting.

She asked to come in—friendly and smiling as she entered my office and laid a folder on my desk.

“The specimen you sent down yesterday was unlike anything I’ve ever seen before,” she said.

I instantly thought of those fleeting moments in the O.R. where I felt like something was pushing back against my instruments. But I didn’t mention any of that.

“How so?”

“I’ve been unable to identify it. It just doesn’t fit any known tissue classifications…” She hesitated. “There’s something else.”

I felt my stomach tighten.

“Can you show me your notes from the surgery?” She asked.

At the moment, I didn’t think to wonder why she needed my notes when I was sitting right in front of her. But in my shock, I turned to my computer and began searching for the documents.

We sat in silence, the only sound that of the keys clicking on my keyboard.

I had nearly found the document when Hannah broke the silence.

“How was the baseball game?”

“It was…” I started. Then froze. I had never told her about—

I looked up. Everything about Hannah was different.

She glared down at me, her face contorted with rage.

That’s when I noticed the scalpel in her hand.

“You should have left me alone!” she shouted, lunging over my desk, swinging the scalpel wildly.

The thing about sharp instruments like a scalpel (and high adrenaline moments) is that you hardly feel the cut, however deep it might be. I struggled with Hannah, trying desperately to keep the blade away from me. But as both of our clothes began showing red stains, I knew I was failing. Thanks to my fearful shouts, security entered the room and, though it took multiple men to subdue her, finally ended the attack.

I was rushed off to get my wounds stitched up. But even as I worried about my own wounds, a frightening thought began to clarify in my mind.

But it was impossible.

As soon as I could free myself from the ER, I walked down to the pathology wing. After a little searching, I found the specimen container for the mass I had removed the day before.

It was empty.

item.title: My New Sister.
item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
I had a lot on my mind as I drove home from Dr. Wroble’s office.

What all this would mean for me, and if I really wanted any of it at all, though I wasn’t sure that mattered too much.

There was also this pressing question about why my room was so important. RYNE was very close to where I slept. I guess he was always close if you lived in Clearview, but the thought wasn’t comforting to me then.

I pulled into the driveway, considering what, if any of this, I should share with my parents. By the time I got to the door, I decided it was best to keep it a secret. So when my mom inevitably asked, I just told her that Dr. Wroble thought the issues with my vision would go away on their own. It was partially true, anyway.

I headed back to my room, but hardly had any time to search for any evidence of RYNE before there was a knock at the door.

I peeked my head out of my room as both my parents answered the door. There, beyond the threshold, stood a young girl with long brown hair and a big smile. She might have been in her early twenties. Standing on the balls of her feet, she beamed excitedly at my parents.

My parents, however, only looked confused.

“Can we help you?”

“Surprise, Mom and Dad!” the girl said. “It’s me, Rachel. I’m back early from Africa.”

The confusion on my parents’ faces melted away into looks of pure joy.

“Oh, Rachel!” my mom shouted. “We missed you. It’s been so long.” She rushed over and gave the girl a hug.

I stood in the hallway, my face scrunching up in confusion with each passing second. My dad joined in the hug.

“I know you two weren’t expecting me,” she said, “but it’s been so many years out there that my supervisor insisted I take some time off from my charity work and visit my family.”

“What great news!” my mom said. “You do such good work out there. We’re so proud of you!”

I wanted to say something, but I couldn’t even think of the words to speak. I was sure I didn’t have a sister in Africa or anywhere else, but the way my parents reacted made me wonder. Were they the crazy ones, or was I?

“Is it okay if I stay here for a few weeks?” she asked. “I know you’re probably using my room for something else, but I can sleep anywhere.”

“Of course, honey,” my dad replied. “You never even need to ask. We’ll find a place for you.”

My parents led the girl inside, and they sat down on the couch. As soon as my mom saw me standing in the hallway, she beckoned me over excitedly.

“Eliot, look! Your sister’s here!”

“Hey, El,” she said, standing up and extending her arms for a hug. “Been a while, eh?”

And as she spoke, memories of a sister flooded back into my mind. It has been a while; I thought.

Then another impulse, stronger than the first, took over.

No. I don’t have a sister. I don’t know who this person is.

And every time she spoke, this battle raged within my mind.

I stood there, stunned, my eyes darting between my parents and the stranger standing in the living room, waiting for a hug.

“Eliot?” said my mom, confusion now settling on her face. “What’s the matter?”

I broke my silence with the only words that could escape my mouth in that moment.

“Who is this?”

Now it was my dad’s turn to speak, an edge in his voice.

“It’s not funny, son,” he said. “Your sister’s been away for a long time. You should at least welcome her back before getting into any jokes.”

Even Rachel’s smile faltered for a moment. Was she confused, too?

“Give your sister a hug, Eliot,” said my mom.

It wasn’t actually that hard to let the I have a sister part of my brain take over for a moment. I laughed, shook my head, and gave the girl a genuine hug, still knowing something was not right.

“Well, let’s sit down,” said my mom. “We want to hear all about your adventures in Africa.”

We all sat on the sofa. I ended up between my parents and Rachel.

As she went over the past half decade, or whatever it was supposed to be since she’d been gone, she spoke about her time in Africa. Botswana, to be exact.

She wove in memories from her time at home, little anecdotes of her experience in high school, or moments between us as siblings. And every time she did, it was almost as if the memory popped into my mind as the words were being spoken.

If I let myself, I could believe them. I could almost see them in my mind’s eye.

But my parents, they didn’t seem to have any choice.

They would even nod along to obviously false stories, like how much our family used to love sledding (we hate the cold) or going out for ice cream. Both my dad and I are lactose intolerant. But history was being rewritten with every word she spoke on that sofa.

It was about an hour of my head spinning through various stories, trying to parse exactly what was going on.

My dad got up to help Rachel unload her car while I followed my mom into the kitchen.

“Mom,” I said, “did anything Rachel said sound strange to you at all?”

“Not really, Eliot,” she replied, getting ingredients out for dinner. “Why do you ask?”

“And do you remember all the stories she told about our time growing up together?”

“Yeah, Eliot. The only thing that feels strange right now are your questions.”

“Do you think you could find an old photo that has Rachel in it? Or maybe some old school papers, anything like that?”

“Well, I’m sure I could,” she said, “if I dug around in the closets. Really, what are you getting at?”

She was getting angry now, but I could see there was really no point to it.

“Nothing, Mom,” I replied. “Do you need any help with food?”

“I’ll manage all right in here, but… can you pull up the blow-up mattress from the basement? Rachel will have to stay in your room until we can figure something else out. It’ll be just like old times.”

She gushed.

My heart sank. For all I knew, this girl was going to kill me in my sleep.

“Why can’t she sleep on the couch?” I asked.

“I am not going to make her sleep on the couch. And I’m not going to make her sleep on an air mattress either. That’s for you. She can have your bed until we find her something better.”

With an angry huff, I stomped downstairs to get the air mattress.

At first, I thought I would sleep in the living room. It would probably be safer. Then I remembered I was supposed to find out what was unique about my room. Not knowing who this girl was or what she wanted, I feared the two might be related, and I should keep a close eye on her.

So I prepared my new bed on the floor of my own bedroom as my dad brought Rachel’s suitcases inside and set them at the foot of my bed.

My mom pulled out all the stops for dinner. I set out the fancy silverware and even opened a bottle of champagne in celebration of Rachel’s return from Botswana.

My parents said goodnight.

Rachel and I were alone for the first time.

“I’m feeling pretty tired too,” she said. “I think I’m going to go lie down.”

Once I had resolved not to leave her alone in my bedroom, I agreed and followed her to get ready for bed.

She kept making small talk as she rummaged through her suitcase, her voice light, almost sing-song, as she pulled out a worn T-shirt and a pair of shorts. She didn’t look at me when she did it.

“And there was this guide,” she was saying, half-laughing to herself, “who swore he could tell when a lion was nearby just by—”

She took off her shirt mid-sentence.

I looked away, then back again, trying to match the natural air Rachel was exuding. But nothing… nothing about any of this was natural.

She kept talking.

Like this was the most normal thing in the world.

It’s one thing to feel like your life is being rewritten in real time, like the past itself is slipping under someone else’s control. It’s another thing entirely when the person doing it moves through your space with that kind of ease.

I didn’t know where to look.

I laughed awkwardly.

“Uh—what are you—”

“Oh, come on, El,” Rachel said, glancing at me now, a grin tugging at the corner of her mouth. “I know it’s been a while, but you’ve seen me in my underwear before. It’s not that big of a deal.”

The way she said it made something in my chest tighten.

“No, I haven’t,” I said, but it came out weaker than I meant it to.

Her eyebrow lifted.

“I haven’t,” I said again, louder now. “I don’t even know who you are.”

Something flickered across her face. It was almost confusion—but then it was gone, replaced by that same amused calm.

By the time I forced myself to look at her again, her pajama shirt was on, her long brown hair caught awkwardly beneath the collar, one hand tugging it free.

She just watched me.

Like she was trying to decide something.

And then the smile came back, slower this time.

“Well then,” she said, tilting her head just slightly, “this is going to be interesting.”

item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
It’s April and I’m back.

Now with a new philosophy on this whole writing thing. It all started with getting off of Spotify (which started from a book I read this winter).

I realized how dependent I’ve become on these big companies which do not have my best interests in mind. Especially those that are adjacent to creativity (Spotify, video streaming services, Amazon (book publishing and all the above)—they have the added harm of separating artists from those that appreciate their work.

I got off of Spotify, and used the money I would have spent on it buying direct from artists I like. What’s more, I’m free from doomscrolling for stuff to listen to. My relationship with music has become much healthier. I want to keep doing this with other services.

Why am I telling you this?

Because I want to apply what I’ve learned to the way I distribute my writing. Big distributors and paywalls are not the way. I don’t know if I’ll ever fully disentangle myself from the Amazon ecosystem, but I’m going to take steps to remove the boundaries between myself and those that happen to read my work.

The first step is removing “paid content” on here. Everything will be free from here on out. Even something so simple (not having to write content for two groups) is very freeing, and it allows me to focus on the writing as opposed to the marketing. I’m going to keep the paid option open for those interested in supporting this project. But even that will not be my preferred method.

If you find any value in my work, return some value to me by clicking the button below. Such buttons will be present in all future posts.

Anesthesia Isn’t What You Think.

The main ingredient in general anesthesia is propofol.

And while I’m a chemist by trade, I’d never given much thought to propofol in my life—until I was scheduled for a surgery. A routine procedure to repair a hernia that had been bothering me for some time.

Like most people facing surgery for the first time, I read up on the anesthesia process. I wanted to know what would happen when I was put under. What I found, at first, was reassuring enough.

But the properties of propofol struck me as… strange.

We all assume that during surgery we don’t feel anything because we’re unconscious. And that’s fine. I had no desire to be awake on an operating table. But propofol doesn’t just make you sleep. It has another effect—one that made me a little uncomfortable.

Besides inducing unconsciousness, propofol is also an amnesiac.

That is, it makes you forget. More precisely, it prevents the brain from encoding memory in the first place.

I’m sure I wasn’t alone in considering the implications of that once I learned it. The question lodged itself in my mind and refused to leave.

What if anesthesia isn’t what we think it is?

What if, far from eliminating pain during surgery, it’s simply a way to ensure you don’t remember how painful it was?

I couldn’t stop picturing myself strapped to the operating table—conscious, aware, feeling everything—while my brain quietly failed to record it. An experience perfectly lived and perfectly erased.

Needless to say, the thought disturbed me.

The more I turned it over, the more it consumed me. Part of it was fear, but part of it was professional curiosity. As a scientist, I wanted an answer. A real one. And there was no way to get it without putting myself at risk.

But I was willing to test it.

You see, it wouldn’t be particularly difficult to design a compound that interfered specifically with propofol’s effect on memory encoding while leaving its other mechanisms untouched. In principle, I could create a drug that—if taken beforehand—would allow me to remember everything.

If anesthesia worked the way we believed it did, the compound would do nothing. I’d be unconscious, and there would be nothing to remember.

But if something else was happening—if consciousness remained—I would know.

I told myself that, as surgeries go, a hernia repair probably wasn’t that bad. Painful, yes, but survivable. And if I did remember something—anything—it would be traumatic, certainly. But it would also be a scientific discovery of enormous importance.

I decided I would take the chance.

With more than a month before my surgery, I got to work mapping out propofol’s pathways and its effects on memory. I learned that its primary impact comes from potentiating GABA_A receptors, increasing chloride influx into neurons and hyperpolarizing post-synaptic membranes. In simple terms, it shuts down the conditions required for memory formation.

My goal was to create a compound that bound to those same receptors but had a dramatically shorter half-life. Long enough to block propofol’s amnesiac effect, but brief enough to clear quickly and allow memory function to resume.

The timing would be critical. I would need to take it shortly before the propofol was administered.

That wasn’t a problem.

I tested the compound on myself, measuring recall and tracking the timing of memory gaps after ingestion. After a week or two of refinement, I had something I believed would work.

The preliminary results were promising.

And that, I told myself, was the most dangerous part. In all likelihood, I was in more danger ingesting my haphazard compounds than I would be from the anesthesia, regardless of how it ended up working. But I had passed that hurdle and was (anxiously) ready for my surgery.

When the day finally came, I tucked the small glass vial containing my compound into my pocket and headed over to the surgery center.

Just before they wheeled me off to the operating room, I downed the liquid… there was no turning back now.

The doctor hooked up my IV and told me to count down from ten. I don’t think I got to five.

The next thing I knew, I was awake—in a different room. I was still on the gurney, and, from the feeling around my groin area, post-operation. But something was wrong. My wrists and ankles were strapped down.

I struggled against my restraints, but couldn’t budge.

Soon though, a man entered the room. He didn’t look like a doctor. He wore jeans and a t-shirt and carried a large tablet under his arm.

“Mr. Jones,” he said. “I’m a technician for [I’m censoring the name of the company for my safety, but it’s a big tech company that you would recognize] and we have purchased the biometric data rights from this surgery center.”

I didn’t know what that meant and was more than a little freaked out. So, I returned to struggling feebly against my restraints.

“Mr. Jones, please. Your surgery was a success. But if you continue like this, you may damage your incision.”

I tried to calm down, but my heart rate was through the roof, and my breathing came in ragged gasps.

“What is this?” I asked.

“I’m just going to collect some data from you, and then you’ll be on your way. Not to worry. You won’t remember a thing.”

He placed his tablet down on his lap and with a few taps, a device on a long arm swiveled from the wall and hovered above me.

The device whirred and flashed as it rotated and projected a grid pattern over my body.

“First, we’ll do some ocular mapping.”

The device moved within inches of my face. I tried to turn away, but something held my head in place. Tiny arms emerged from the device and grabbed onto each of my eyelids, holding them open. The machine emitted a series of flashes, whirrs and beeps as it hovered over my eyes.

“Now we’ll collect a sample of vitreous humor.”

I didn’t know what that was when he said it, but soon discovered, to my horror, that it’s the fluid in your eye.

A small door on the device hissed open, and the long needle approached my eye with a metallic glint.

I screamed. I struggled. But ultimately, I stared helplessly as the needle pierced my eye. The pain was excruciating.

Another beep, and the needle retracted.

“On to gastrointestinal data.” The man spoke so casually, as if he had done this hundreds of times. He probably had.

A long cylindrical apparatus emerged from the device, and without warning rammed itself into my mouth. I could feel the cold metal snaking down my throat, muffling my screams. It felt like that thing was inside me for an eternity. And when it emerged, it was covered in clear, viscous goop.

“We got your blood while we were in there. Time for bone marrow.”

The device hovered over my right leg, just out of my range of sight. I heard the unmistakable sound of a drill whiz to life and felt a shooting pain in my thigh.

“Alright. Almost done,” the man said. “Just one more thing…”

Now we get to the part that I’m not even comfortable sharing anonymously. I’ll have to leave it to your imagination.

“Alright, Mr. Jones, all done. Time to go back to sleep. When you wake up, this will all be gone.”

I knew he was wrong. So, as I was drifting back to sleep, I had to ask.

“What’s this all for?”

“With all this data, we’ll be able to show you some killer ads.”

I woke up in a normal recovery room. All the doctors and nurses acted as if nothing had happened.

Those ads had better be good.

“Okay,” I replied. “But what does that have to do with me?”

Dr. Wroble laughed. “I thought you’d like to know a bit about RYNE, now that you’re connected to him.”

For all I knew about RYNE, being any more connected to it than I already was felt like an unwelcome development.

“Can’t I do something to stop it?”

“I’m not sure. I’ve never tried. But you may find RYNE to be more of an ally than anything else.”

I took a breath. “Graham said something like that too.”

Dr. Wroble made a face I couldn’t quite decipher. “He would say that, since he has a monopoly on the conduits. He thinks RYNE works for him. But it’s more complicated than that.”

“I thought you said there were no other conduits,” I said.

“No more conduits with any agency. People like you and me. RYNECORP started making their own, and things got messy.”

He didn’t need to elaborate. I’d seen them—the people (were they even people?) kept behind glass in the basement of the RYNECORP building. The Oil Man. Principal O’Neil. The Librarian. And who knew how many others?

But I didn’t need to know who they were. I needed to know what they were. And, by consequence, who I was.

“But… why?”

“The way I’ve begun to think about it,” he said, “RYNE is like a fungus. If you see a mushroom sprouting from the ground, you know there’s a network of mycelium beneath it. The real organism is invisible. RYNE is the mycelium. Conduits are the mushrooms.”

I scrunched my face in disgust. I didn’t want to be a mushroom.

“Perhaps not the most endearing example, my little mushroom.” He winked. “All I mean is that conduits are how RYNE interacts with the world above ground. It used to be that they were normal people—like you and me. Now they’re almost entirely under RYNECORP’s control.”

I had a million questions, but one rose above the rest.

“If you’re not like the other conduits… why do you come off so—”

“Like this?” he asked, sliding his glasses back on. Once again, he became the eerie man I’d met at the beginning of my appointment.

“Uh… yeah.”

Dr. Wroble laughed and removed the glasses again.

“I guess it’s easier just to fit the bill. I’d stand out more if I wasn’t a little strange. Maybe not to the regular folks around here, but certainly to the execs at RYNECORP.”

I started another question, but Dr. Wroble interrupted.

“I know there’s a lot you’d like to ask, Eliot. And I’m happy to teach you what I know. But we’ve got something a bit more pressing to deal with first. It’s about your bedroom…”

That was probably the last thing I expected him to say. My confusion showed.

“You’ve been connecting with RYNE in your bedroom. The school makes sense; Clearview High is a hot spot. But unless your house is somewhere unusual, you shouldn’t be having any issues there.”

Dr. Wroble pulled out a map, very similar to the one I saw in Principal O’Neil’s office. It had the layout of the town, but additional markings all over to show where RYNE was most concentrated.

He pointed to my neighborhood.

“Not much going on there. Not to say RYNE can’t be moving. He’s always growing. But I think I’d know about it. Something else is going on.”

While Dr. Wroble’s interest in my bedroom was flattering… I think. The more pressing question to me was what the heck is happening to me, and what does it mean for me that I’m a conduit? Reasonable enough, questions, I thought. But despite a few additional attempts to get some clarity, Dr. Wroble was fixated on this bedroom issue.

“Go home and do some investigating—find out how RYNE is linked to your bedroom. Come back when you have something to share.”

And just like that, I was dismissed.

I had come to Dr. Wroble’s office to fix my eyes. I left not knowing who—or what—I even was.

item.title: A Short History of Clearview
item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
[This is some short bonus content for those supporting the project. The story continues on 2/5 with Dr. Wroble Pt. 2—a free release]

I stood there, staring at Dr. Wroble, wondering what any of this meant. About a thousand questions raced through my mind, but I only managed to blink at him, mouth agape.

“I think we should start with a little history lesson, Eliot.”

Dr. Wroble closed the box lying on the floor and beckoned me to the office side of the room. He sat down behind the big wooden desk and bade me sit on the other side.

“Clearview isn’t like other towns,” he said.

The understatement made me laugh for the first time since arriving.

“Three major events contributed to the unique nature of this town. The first, and most important, was the arrival of Rynehold Morgan somewhere in the 1920s.”

Dr. Wroble opened a desk drawer and found an old photograph of a man standing next to a large contraption. It looked something like an overcomplicated engine, covered in glass tubes and copper pipes.

“Dr. Morgan was driven west from his home in New York because his research made him very unpopular. He ended up in what became the town of Clearview.”

“What did he research?” I asked.

“Not much of it survives in written form. But that doesn’t matter, because we still have Dr. Morgan here with us… in a way.”

“Rynehold Morgan,” I muttered, staring at the photo atop the desk. “You mean?”

“RYNE is a person… or at least, what remains of one.”

I shuddered.

“Whatever Dr. Morgan did to himself—whether his experiment was a success or a catastrophic failure—the seed of RYNE was planted right here under our feet.”

“What do you mean, seed?” I asked.

“Things get a little blurry in the sources during this time. But I know that RYNE was at one point quite small and localized. Perhaps only the size of a normal human being. It survived untouched in the old Rynehold Manor for decades, until the second event that played a critical role in the development of our town: the end of World War II.”

“Little pockets of suburbia were popping up all over America, and during this time, Clearview was founded. The old manor was preserved and, for a brief period, became a museum before sitting vacant for another two decades.”

Dr. Wroble paused and met my eyes.

“The next important event happened in the ’80s. Can you guess what that was, Eliot?”

“RYNECORP?”

“Exactly. Somehow word of RYNE got out, and the site of the manor became the RYNECORP campus. And that’s when things got messy.”

They already seemed pretty messy to me…

“I don’t know exactly how they did it, but RYNECORP began feeding and modifying RYNE. They suspected RYNE could be useful for industry. And before long, RYNE was larger than the town itself.”

“What did RYNE do for RYNECORP?”

“For one, RYNE protects their intellectual property. As you know, there’s a pretty serious rivalry between RYNECORP and HaleTech Industries. RYNE gives RYNECORP a leg up in all that corporate espionage crap. But there’s something more. RYNE has become the neural network of the entire town. He connects us all. So it’s no exaggeration to say that the scientists and engineers at RYNECORP are using all our brains, to some extent, in their work.”

I thought of the day I encountered RYNE for the first time in the basement of the RYNECORP building. The voice in the speaker: RYNE knows your thoughts. It looks like he not only knows them, but somehow uses them too.

item.title: Dr. Wroble Pt. 1
item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
It was early February of my senior year of high school when the trouble with my eyes began.

It came in spells.

Most of the time my vision was fine, but when it hit, I knew something was wrong. My sight blurred. My eyes throbbed, and I saw motion that wasn’t there.

During those spells, I might be looking at my desk or watching TV at home, when suddenly I’d see things moving—subtle, distant motion—like something shifting just out of focus. But when the blurriness faded, so did the movement.

I told my parents about it, and at first they were hopeful it would just go away. In Clearview, most of us treated the eye doctor as a last resort. The stories surrounding that office made people reluctant to make an appointment. But I kept complaining, and eventually I reached a point where anything felt better than continuing to deal with it.

So my mom called Dr. Wroble’s office and got me an appointment for the next day.

She offered to drive me, but I assured her I’d be fine. Besides, the appointment got me out of school, which was a welcome bonus.

The next day, in the middle of fourth period, I left class and walked out to the parking lot where my car waited. The lot was desolate, as was the drive to Dr. Wroble’s office. The eerie quiet of Clearview in the middle of the day stirred up memories of the stories I’d heard—about the office and about Dr. Wroble himself.

There were stories of patients looking through his instruments and seeing increasingly gruesome or deeply unwelcome scenes involving themselves or their families. Stories about the eye drops—drops that let you see creatures that weren’t really there, but also caused weeks of your life to slip by as though they were minutes.

Most of the stories focused on Dr. Wroble himself: his round, flat glasses, which often obscured his eyes behind a thick glare, and his smile—a smile that made you crave to be anywhere else.

Still, for all the uncanny rumors surrounding his practice, no one ever questioned his competence. He fixed eyes. And I hoped he would fix mine.

I pulled into the strip mall where Dr. Wroble’s office sat between a Chinese food restaurant and a Weight Watchers. I parked in the nearly empty lot and walked through the glass storefront into his practice.

The waiting room was empty. A sliding mirror, where the receptionist presumably sat, was closed. I never actually saw her during my visit.

I wrote my name on a sign-in sheet, clipped it to the clipboard on the front desk, and sat down to wait.

A moment later, the mirror slid open. A thin, bony hand reached out, took the clipboard, and the mirror slid shut again.

I tried to distract myself with the outdated magazines on the coffee table, but it wasn’t long before the door opened.

Dr. Wroble stood there, dressed entirely in white, peering at me through the thick lenses of his glasses.

“Eliot,” he said.

I gave him a polite smile and stood to follow him down the hall. The office itself looked like any other doctor’s office I’d been to—sterile fluorescent lighting, muted colors, and anatomical posters showing body parts and the things that could go wrong with them.

He led me into a dimly lit room filled with instruments and equipment. I sat down in a large chair facing the machines.

Dr. Wroble pulled up a chair beside me and sat down.

“So, Eliot,” he said, “I hear we’re having some trouble with our eyes. Can you tell me what’s been going on?”

I tried to look at him through the glare of his round glasses, but I could only look for so long until I averted my eyes.

“Well,” I said, trying to ignore his overall creepy demeanor, “my vision keeps getting blurry. And when it does, I feel like I’m seeing things that aren’t really there.”

“Does this happen in any place or at any time in particular?”

“Now that I think about it,” I replied, “it happens when I’m at school and in my room. I don’t remember it happening anywhere else.”

“School makes sense,” he muttered to himself. “But the room...”

Dr. Wroble closed his eyes and rubbed his chin with his palm. After a moment, he began nodding, as if having made up his mind about something. He took off his glasses and looked me in the eye.

Removing the glasses was like he had taken off a mask. The man who had seconds ago been unsettling now looked perfectly normal. Perhaps even friendly.

“I think I may know what’s causing your issue,” said Dr. Wroble. “But there’s a test that will tell us for sure. Come with me.”

We exited the room, but instead of turning back toward the entrance, we continued down the hall until we reached a door that looked unlike the others. It was old and wooden, featuring a large brass doorknob. Dr. Wroble opened the door and led me through. The room looked like an office, but only half of it. The other half was empty, but for the small wooden box at the far end of the white-tiled floor.

“Stand here, Eliot,” Dr. Wroble said, motioning to a spot on the floor across from the box.

Obediently, I moved to the spot. Though the nerves I felt earlier had crept back in. This felt nothing like an eye exam.

“Any vision problems?”

I shook my head.

“Take a step forward... Anything?”

“Nope,” I replied.

“One more.”

As I took another step, my vision blurred worse than ever before. And the movements, they were clearer. Whatever was moving was in that box, throughout the walls and under my feet.

Dr. Wroble must have noticed my shock because he never even asked me about my vision.

“I thought so,” he said.

Then I felt something on my hand. Dr. Wroble had reached out and grabbed it. Gently.

My vision returned to normal.

“What happened?” I asked through heavy breaths.

“It looks like you may be a conduit.”

“A what?” I asked, not expecting my eye condition to include me being anything.

Dr. Wroble pulled me by my hand toward the box.

“Open it.”

I looked over to Dr. Wroble, whose face was calm and reassuring. He said nothing else, but gave me a slow nod.

I leaned over with my free arm and grasped the lid of the box. Slowly, I lifted the lid and recoiled when I saw what was inside. The movement I saw while in my blurry spell now played out in front of me. A fleshy tendril, that I had reluctantly come to know as a part of RYNE, pulsed in the box before me, slowly passing through two holes in the bottom of the box, as if a snake slithering from one side to the other.

“It’s okay, Eliot,” Dr. Wroble said. “It won’t hurt you.”

I stood before the open box, staring at the thing inside.

“Touch it.”

I shuddered, but reached out and moved my shaking hand toward the box. When my fingers met the tendril, Dr. Wroble let go of my hand. In an instant, my vision went hazy again. Everything in front of me faded away, and flashes of other scenes passed before my eyes. I saw the insides of houses, hallways in my school, and roads I recognized from around town. None of the visions lasted long; each one came quick on the heels of the last.

This continued until I felt Dr. Wroble’s hand on my wrist, pulling my arm away from RYNE.

“What did you see?” he asked.

My eyes burned; my breath was ragged. I struggled to find the words to explain what I saw.

“Everything,” I said.

Dr. Wroble’s face lit up.

“Finally,” he said. “Another conduit.” He exhaled, something like relief in his voice. “It’s been lonely being the only one left for the last decade.”

item.title: The Dead End
item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
[scroll to the bottom for a free book]

Of all the streets in my town, there was only one dead end. The only problem was, it was never in the same place.

Part of childhood in Clearview was learning about some of the town’s idiosyncrasies. Little do’s and don’ts that kept you safe and out of uncomfortable situations. And as soon as I was old enough to go out around my neighborhood on my bike, my parents sat me down and told me about the dead end.

“Beth,” my mom said as I was putting my helmet on. “If you ever run into the dead end, don’t go past the barrier. Just turn around and ride in a different direction.”

“I’m just riding in our neighborhood, Mom,” I replied. “There’s no dead end.”

She gave me a look. “Just stay out of it if you see it, okay?”

I assured my mom I’d heed her warning and shot down the driveway, ready to enjoy my little taste of freedom.

And that day, everything was normal as could be. I rode around for a while and returned home happy as can be.

But it wasn’t long before my mom’s admonition came in handy. One beautiful summer afternoon, I was out riding my bike when I turned a corner and everything was different. I should have seen Mrs. Roberts’s house on the left and that house with all the dogs on the right. But I didn’t see any houses at all. I had finally encountered the dead end.

It wasn’t much to look at. The asphalt ended at one of those metal highway barriers, beyond which was a tall sand mound and some trees. As uncomfortable as it was to have the geography of your neighborhood shift before your eyes, there was nothing particularly frightening about it. Still, I did exactly as instructed, turned around, and pedaled in the opposite direction. Later on, I rode past the spot and everything was back to normal. No problem.

This happened to me a few times that summer, and each time everything resolved when I turned around and rode away.

Until it didn’t.

It was a cool and cloudy day, one of the first days where autumn’s arrival felt imminent.

I rode my bike to the end of my street, but quickly turned around. I was underdressed for the temperature and wanted to grab a sweatshirt. So, back to my house I pedaled. As I rounded a bend only a few houses from my own, I ran into the dead end.

I huffed in frustration. The dead end, which was once ominous, was now merely an inconvenience—one more obstacle between me and warm attire. Plus, the only way back to my house was miles longer and through streets I wasn’t even allowed to ride on.

Still, my plan was to turn around, ride for a few minutes, and simply return to where I needed to go. The dead end would be gone. It always was before long.

My first trek out was only five minutes. Goosebumps were forming on my arms and legs, and I really wanted to get home. I returned to my street. No luck. It was still there.

So I went out for a longer time. By now, I was very cold and very impatient. Returning to the spot, I found the dead end still hadn’t moved from its place.

I stood there staring at the barrier, wondering if my house wasn’t just over that sand mound.

Soon, my exasperation won out. I parked my bike in front of my neighbor’s house and approached the dead end. I was just going to look—nothing more.

I stepped over the metal barrier and trudged up the sand mound. Relief washed over me as soon as I could see the other side. Beyond a few trees, the rest of my neighborhood sat, just as normal.

I didn’t think twice. Running down the sand mound, I passed the trees and was in my driveway within a minute. Nothing looked different. Nothing was out of place.

“Mom, I’m just here to grab a sweatshirt!” I yelled as I passed through the front door.

No answer.

I ran to my room, threw on an extra layer, and headed back toward the front door.

“I’m heading back out, Mom!”

Still nothing.

It was unusual for my mom not to answer. It was a small house. Even if she were in the bathroom, she would have heard me.

“Mom?”

For the first time since I passed through the dead end, something felt wrong.

With a pit in my stomach, I stepped back into the living room. Slowly, I approached my parents’ room and peeked my head around the doorframe.

I gasped.

There on the floor lay my mom. My first instinct was to run, and I made it halfway back through the house before the thought even occurred to me that I should help her.

With all the courage I could muster, I returned to the room, stepped inside, and kneeled over my mother.

She was dead.

I had never seen a dead body before in my life, but I had seen dead animals on the side of the road in various states of decomposition. From close up, my mother looked more like the roadkill I had seen than her former self.

Her skin was pale, her face gaunt, and her eyes were sunken in. Her hair was thin and fell in matted locks.

I lost it.

Through tears and heaving breaths, I sprinted from the room. Running to the phone on the kitchen wall, I picked up the receiver and dialed 911, unsure I would be able to speak when someone picked up.

The phone rang. And rang. And rang. Until finally, the ringing stopped, and silence took over the line.

“Hello?” I sniffled into the receiver.

Then I felt something cold grab my arm from behind. I turned around and saw my mother, still decaying, staring down at me through white, lifeless eyes.

I screamed and beat my mom’s hand off me with the receiver of the phone. Once free, I took off. Mom made a noise somewhere between a gurgle and a moan and followed me, hobbling, toward the front door.

I shot down the driveway and into the street, back toward the dead end. But it wasn’t there. Still, my bike sat where I had left it before I crossed over the sand mound. As I ran toward my bike, I noticed movement in the houses I passed.

Slowly, lumbering out of front doors, were the undead versions of my neighbors. Mr. Ken, who was over four hundred pounds, pressed himself through the doorway, losing a slab of flesh from his side as he emerged from his home. Mrs. Parkinson still had on her nightgown and carried a bottle of red wine within her skeletal fingers.

Everyone bore some resemblance to their former selves, but everyone was clearly dead, and everyone was chasing after me.

I jumped onto my bike and raced down the road as my transformed neighbors poured onto their front lawns.

My only hope (though I had no idea if it would work) was to find the dead end again and pass back over. But as I sped along, that became increasingly difficult. The streets were growing crowded with lumbering corpses. And while they were slow, if I got knocked off my bike, I was done for.

After a few turns, to my immense relief, the dead end came into sight. Perhaps I got careless seeing my salvation, but somehow I rode too close to the outstretched arm of one of my neighbors. I lost balance, skidded to the ground and, despite the pain, scrambled to my feet in a mad dash to the dead end.

I dodged grabbing hands and snapping jaws, receiving more than a few scratches as I clambered over the divider and up the sand mound.

Throwing myself over, I sprinted through the trees and into the street. It was empty.

I fell to the ground, gasping and panting. My chest felt like it was going to explode.

When I could manage to stand, I found my bike and pedaled home.

Cautiously, I opened my front door and shouted inside.

“Mom?”

“Yes, honey?”

Mom’s voice was normal. I rushed over to her and gave her a hug. Not wanting to scare her, I just told her I fell off my bike and kept it at that.

She tended my wounds, and we made brownies together that evening. But as we worked, I noticed that she kept grabbing her right wrist.

“Did you hurt your wrist, Mom?” I asked.

“I’m not sure what happened,” she replied. “It feels like I hit it on something. But I don’t remember hurting it at all.”

item.title: My co-worker doesn't exist. But he saved my life.
item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
In the summer leading up to my senior year of high school, I got my first job working at “Film Fanatics,” Clearview’s movie rental place.

It was a pretty sweet job. The work was simple, and you got a free rental every week. And besides re-shelving returns and checking people out at the front register, most of the “job” was just sitting around.

The only negative was that each shift only had one worker, so the downtime could get sort of boring.

A bonus was that, for the first month or so, things were pretty normal. That wasn’t a given in my town. The only thing that I found a little odd was the end cap that faced the register. It had a single shelf labeled “Ben Recommends,” and on the shelf sat two DVDs. Always two. Though the selection varied week to week.

Such a setup wouldn’t seem odd at a movie rental store if not for the fact that nobody named “Ben” worked at my store. I asked the workers who came in for the shift after mine, and they had no idea. I even asked Mr. Carson (whose name also isn’t Ben), the store’s owner. His answer was a little unsettling.

He leaned over and with a hushed voice said, “Best not to ask, Eliot.”

I didn’t know what to make of it, but it was such a small thing, I mostly forgot about it.

Still, since I basically had to stare at the shelf all day while I sat at the front desk, I couldn’t help but notice the titles on display.

And it was during our town’s annual 4th of July festival that I first noticed the connection between “Ben’s Recommendations” and the events going on around me.

I had volunteered to walk along the fire company’s float and throw candy out to the kids in the crowd. And as we were prepping everything before the parade, I overheard the fire chief talking to someone.

“It’s a shame we won’t be doing these anymore,” he said.

“What?” I interrupted.

“The mayor announced it earlier. Budget cuts. This will be the last parade.”

The two movies that were sitting on the shelf at Film Fanatics:

“Independence Day,” and “The Last Parade.”

I tried to justify it at first. Perhaps whoever was setting up the display just knew about the cancellation in advance.

But now that I was aware, the coincidences just kept happening.

A few weeks later, I was ringing up a customer and all of a sudden, the register died. No lights, nothing happened when I turned it off and back on, just dead. I finished the transaction in cash, logged the rental to enter it into the computer later and picked up the phone to call Mr. Carson. But as the phone was ringing, my eyes wandered over to the end-cap.

One of the movies on the shelf was titled: “Out of Order.”

Had that been there all day? I just didn’t remember.

Another time, I was checking out a particularly large customer. Despite the air conditioning, the man was sweating profusely, nearly soaking the movie jacket and the cash he handed me. It was pretty gross.

I was just finishing up with him when I looked over his shoulder and noticed the movie staring back at me:

“The Big One”

I let out a laugh.

“Excuse me?” the man said, looking offended.

I did my best to disguise it as a cough, apologized and prayed that he wouldn’t turn around and notice what I had seen.

Though it was funny, that particular instance was troubling, because I knew that movie had not been on the shelf earlier that day.

Still, what could I do about it? If anything, I thought, it could be helpful.

I didn’t know how right I was.

It was late September; the days were shorter, and because of school, all of my shifts were in the evening. I was taking over for Mr. Carson, who felt it necessary to tell me a little tidbit of news he had heard a few hours before. Someone had escaped from the state hospital. The police were out looking for him. It wasn’t comforting news at the beginning of a long, lonesome shift.

Within the first hour of work, a customer came in and immediately, I knew something was off. He was tall and thin—but not a healthy sort of thin. Veins pulsed in his neck as his eyes darted throughout the store. He was carrying one of those portable DVD players. This was the guy.

“Give me the best movie.” he said, his voice quavering

“What?”

“The best movie…”

I didn’t give much thought to his request. I really just wanted him gone. So I picked out The Godfather, and sent him on his way. I didn’t even check him out. I’d happily pay the cost to get him far away.

Happy to be done with that, I went on with my evening, uncomfortable and constantly checking out the front window. But, for the next four hours everything was fine. I finally started to relax a little.

It was just after nine, and I was sitting at the reception desk, leafing through a magazine waiting for the end of my shift. That’s when I heard something fall to the ground. Looking up, I noticed the “Ben Recommends” shelf only had one movie. The other had fallen to the floor, face down. I stood up and walked over to the fallen case, nerves churning in my stomach. Picking the movie off the floor, I finally saw the title:

“Run”

I didn’t think. I didn’t question it. I just bolted to the front door. But I was too late. The man from earlier was storming toward the entrance, his face full of crazed fury.

I scrambled back into the store when suddenly the lights went out.

The front door flew open, and the man unleashed a torrent of threats and swears.

“I’m going to kill you!” he screamed. “This was NOT the best movie!”

I ducked down between rows of movies, the dim glow from the exit sign painting everything a reddish hue. Trying to track the man’s location by his incessant screaming, I did my best to stay hidden, weaving between rows, working my way toward the exit.

But suddenly, the screaming stopped.

My heavy breathing sounded like a foghorn through the silence.

I tried desperately to keep quiet. To listen. But I couldn’t hear anything besides my own heartbeat and my ragged breaths, which just wouldn’t shut up.

I had to do something.

Slowly, I crept toward the end of an aisle and peeked around the corner.

A hand shot out and grabbed me by the throat.

The man hurled me to the ground and pinned me with his legs as both hands wrapped around my throat.

I tried to pull him off. I tried to punch and flail, but the man’s crazed strength was unlike anything I’d ever experienced. I couldn’t stop it.

My vision was fading along the periphery. And the last thing I would see is this man’s bulging eyes and manic grimace staring down at me.

Was this how I was going to die, because of a bad move recommendation?

Suddenly, the lights flashed on, and the burglar alarm sounded. Contrasted with the dark silence, this new state of things was jolting, even to me, who was in the process of having my life strangled away. The man shot his head up and loosened his grip. He looked around nervously, got up and rushed from the store.

I took a long moment to collect myself. I’m not too proud to say that I broke down in tears once I had registered everything. Fortunately, I had collected myself before the police cars appeared out front to investigate the alarm. The alarm that nobody had set off.

I reported what had happened to the police, and they stuck around as I locked up the store. As I was getting things together, I took another look at “Ben Recommends.” This time, there weren’t DVDs on the shelf at all. Instead, a solitary, unlabeled VHS tape.

I picked it up, threw it in my bag and headed home.

During my long discussion with my parents about what had happened, we got a call from a police officer reporting that the man who had attacked me had been apprehended. We all breathed easily.

But I wasn’t done thinking about all this. I dug our old VCR out of the basement and plugged it into the TV in my bedroom.

Nervously, I inserted the tape and watched the screen flicker to life.

It was footage from the security camera at work. It was me.

I saw myself restocking shelves, walking to and from the front desk. But then I saw someone else. Another guy around my age. At first, I thought it was a customer. But he too was organizing shelves. We were chatting. Laughing. At one point, the guy opened up a box of candy from the front register and shared some with me.

The only problem was, none of this ever happened. Or, at least I don’t remember it…

I watched myself working and interacting with this other guy in disbelief. Beyond my confusion, I was a little sad that I didn’t have a friend to spend those long shifts with.

After a while, the guy picked up a DVD from one of the shelves and walked over to the “Ben Recommends” end-cap. He placed the DVD on the shelf, turned to the camera with a big smile on his face and waved.

I could just make out the title of the movie.

Stand By Me.

item.title: Stranded in Plainfield
item.dc:creator: Matt Benjamin
item.content:encoded:
Eliot picked me up at five on the night of the game.

It was already dark out, and bitterly cold. Even though sports games weren’t his thing, the fact that I’d lost nearly half of my senior year of high school made him more willing to give in and take me.

He met me at the front door, and we hurried through the freezing air to his already-warm, running car. That, too was new. The last time we’d really been hanging out, over the summer, I was the only one with a car. But his job at the movie rental store had finally earned him enough money to buy one of his own—an old Ford Taurus. It was junk, but I couldn’t talk. My car was too.

We drove down Route 7 and out of town. There was nothing but farmland and cornfields between the towns of Clearview and Plainfield, but they may as well have been a brick wall. People only crossed from one town to the other when they had a really good reason.

Clearview and Plainfield had a visceral—and sometimes dangerous—rivalry. And it wasn’t just about sports. That had come later. The feud really began because Clearview’s largest business, RYNECORP, and Plainfield’s HaleTech Industries were bitter enemies. But the sports rivalry certainly didn’t help.

“So how are you feeling?” Eliot asked, placing a hand on my knee as we drove through the cornfields.

“I feel fine,” I shrugged. “It’s weird not remembering such a long stretch of time, but I’m just glad I made it out at all.”

“Well, I missed you,” he said, smiling.

“I bet I missed you too,” I replied. Honestly, I wasn’t sure what was going through my mind during that time.

He laughed, and we drove on, finally crossing the town line into Plainfield.

Everything felt different here. It’s hard to explain the exact vibe, but if I had to choose one word, it would be straight. The buildings were neatly lined up and symmetrical. The roads hardly ever curved. Even the houses felt different—white and boxy, like little laboratories—nothing like the homes back in Clearview.

Eliot shuddered as he made his way through town.

“This place gives me the creeps,” he said.

Even I was starting to wonder if we shouldn’t have just waited for a home game.

But within a few minutes, we were pulling into the parking lot at Plainfield High School. We got out of the car and hurried through the frosty air into the large, industrial-looking building. For all the sterile architecture, the inside of the school felt like any other high school—wide hallways, glass cases filled with sports awards and photos of notable alumni, and clearly marked signs directing people toward the gym where the basketball game was about to start.

Eliot and I walked down the hall and into the gym as both teams were on their respective sides of the court, practicing and warming up. There were a few other students from Clearview there, along with the parents of the players, but our side of the bleachers felt relatively empty compared to theirs.

Typically, the Clearview–Plainfield rivalry went something like this: we won most of the football games in the fall, and they won most of the basketball games in the winter. By spring, the rivalry fizzled out, since no one really cared much about track and field or tennis. Heck, I hardly cared, and Eliot was on the tennis team.

So as the game began, we fully expected to watch a loss.

But as basketball games go, it turned out to be a fun one. The score stayed tight through the fourth quarter, and even though we still lost, it was anyone’s game until the very end.

When it was over, Eliot and I hurried back to his car. It felt even colder than before. We talked briefly about getting something to eat, but neither of us wanted to stay in Plainfield any longer than necessary. We agreed on a place back in Clearview.

It should have been a normal night. Honestly, it would’ve been a great one—if not for what happened next.

We were halfway out of Plainfield when Eliot’s car began to sputter. He pulled over, turned off the ignition, and popped the hood.

“Let me see if there’s anything obvious,” he said, stepping out into the darkness.

Unless Eliot had learned something about fixing cars since the last time I’d seen him, I knew there probably wasn’t anything he could do. A moment later, he climbed back into the driver’s seat.

“I can’t tell anything,” he said. “Let’s just baby it back into town. Maybe my dad can fix it.”

He turned the key. The engine cranked, but never caught. He tried again. And again. Each attempt sounded weaker than the last.

“What’s the plan?” I asked.

I was already fully aware that any plan would involve something I didn’t want to do.

“I guess we need to find a phone,” he said. “We’ll call my dad and get picked up.”

He pointed off to the side of the road. Just beyond us was a neighborhood.

“I guess we’ll knock on a door.”

I definitely didn’t want to do that. But I also definitely didn’t want to sit alone in a stalled car, in the freezing cold, in the middle of Plainfield. So with a huff, I got out, and we walked toward the houses.

I’d mentioned earlier how peculiar the houses in Plainfield looked. What made it worse—especially at night—was that each one had an identical bluish porch light. The effect made everything feel sterile, almost clinical. There were no noticeable differences between the houses, and the cold made us want to get this over with as quickly as possible.

So, we knocked on the first door we came to.

A moment later, an elderly woman answered. She wore a nightgown, her hair set in rollers.

“I’m sorry to bother you, ma’am,” Eliot said, “but our car broke down. Could we possibly use your phone?”

She smiled. “Absolutely.”

She opened the door wide and ushered us in. “Come in, come in. Get out of the cold.”

She led us to a nearby couch.

“So,” she asked, heading toward another room, “where are you kids coming from?”

“We’re from Clearview,” Eliot said.

The moment the word left his mouth, we both knew we’d made a mistake.

She froze, then slowly turned around. Her smile was still there—but it was different.

“Clearview, you say.”

She sat down in an armchair near the door. I felt Eliot shift uncomfortably on the couch next to me.

“What brings you here?” she asked.

“Oh—just a basketball game,” Eliot said.

“Ah. Basketball. My grandson plays basketball.”

She kept talking, asking questions, but I couldn’t stop watching her hand as it reached beneath the nearby end table. I thought I heard a click. It was subtle.

She smiled again. “Oh, look at me, talking when I should be getting you a phone. Just give me a moment… I’ll be right back.”

She left the room.

Eliot and I looked at each other. Neither of us said anything, but the strangeness hung thick in the air. I stood up and crept toward the end table. Stooping down, I saw a small red button mounted underneath its surface.

“We have to go,” I whispered.

We rushed to the front door, but it wouldn’t budge. No matter what we did with the locks on our side, it wouldn’t open.

Eliot yanked aside the curtain on the window next to the door.

The porch light—blue when we’d arrived—was now red.

And out in the yard, a black vehicle was pulling up, its headlights off.

“What’s going on?” I asked.

“I don’t know,” Eliot said. “But we need to get out of here.”

We ran through the house, past the old woman—now seated calmly at her dining room table, not searching for a phone at all. She watched us without speaking as we threw open the back door, which was mercifully unlocked.

We burst into the backyard, vaulted a fence, and tore through neighboring yards. Through backyards and empty streets we ran, watching dark vehicles swarm the neighborhood behind us.

We had no idea where we were going, or how we’d ever make it back to Clearview. We didn’t know who was after us, or why. But I knew that it wasn’t good.

Breathless, we pushed toward a more commercial area: strip malls and storefronts, most of them closed. The emptiness only made us more visible.

Eliot grabbed my hand and pulled me behind one of the buildings. We ran past dumpsters and parked cars as a pair of headlights flared against the wall ahead of us.

Then there was nowhere left to run.

Cornered, still holding my hand, Eliot turned to face the man stepping out of the car. He was dressed entirely in black, the only white showing at his collar beneath a black tuxedo and tie. He raised a pistol and aimed it at us as he approached.

“I guess it was worth trying to run,” he said—then stopped.

He stared at Eliot.

Silence stretched between them. Eliot stared back, as if the two of them were trying to place each other.

Finally, the man spoke again.

“You’re the kid from the jail, aren’t you?”

Eliot didn’t answer. He just nodded.

The man thought for a moment, then shook his head.

“You’re damn lucky, kid,” he said. “Get in the car. I’ll drive you home.”

He lowered the gun and opened the back door. Without hesitation, Eliot pulled me with him and we got in.

The man didn’t speak as he drove us out of Plainfield, through cornfields and farmland, back toward Clearview. Eliot gave directions to his house. We got out, and the man rolled down his window.

“We’re even now,” he said. Then he pulled away.

Eliot’s dad drove me home that night. The next morning, they hired a tow truck to retrieve Eliot’s car.

It was the last time I ever voluntarily set foot in Plainfield.
